key_insight: The paper argues that you can predict whether a base model is worth expensive agentic coding post-training before you actually train it. Instead of relying on end-to-end pass@K alone, it focuses on signals that better reflect whether the model can support multi-step tool use and coding behavior.
problem_solved: It addresses the difficulty of choosing promising base checkpoints for costly agentic post-training in coding tasks. Standard pass@K-style evaluation is a poor predictor because many base models fail at reliable tool invocation, even when they may contain useful coding competence.
method: Compare base checkpoints using evaluation signals designed for agentic coding, not just end-to-end success rates.
Use short-horizon or single-shot task formulations to reduce failures caused by multi-step tool-calling breakdowns.
Predict which checkpoints are most likely to benefit from post-training, enabling better checkpoint selection before expensive training runs.
impact: This helps practitioners spend compute on the base models most likely to improve after agentic training. It can reduce wasted training runs and make model development for coding agents faster and more efficient.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing base checkpoint -> evaluation signals -> predicted post-training utility -> agentic coding agent
Side-by-side comparison chart of pass@K versus short-horizon predictive metrics
Icon set for tools, code editor, and multi-step agent loop to illustrate tool-calling failures
Ranking plot of checkpoints by predicted versus actual post-training performance
paper_title: Before They Can Solve: Predicting Post-Training Coding-Agent Performance from Base Models
paper_authors: Tan Yu, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Jennifer Williams, Zirui Liu
